tier_reason: The README and docs/tpde-llvm/main.md state the 10-20x compile-time win over the LLVM -O0 back-end (first-party, no methodology), and the evaluation is in a peer-reviewed CGO 2026 paper with a Zenodo artifact (SPEC CPU 2017, x86-64 and AArch64 images); the paper, artifact and CGO page were seen only through search snippets (arxiv.org, home.cit.tum.de, 2026.cgo.org, discourse.llvm.org blocked), and SPEC is proprietary with hardware and flags unseen, so not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: TPDE-LLVM compiles 10--20x faster than LLVM -O0 with similar code quality. docs/tpde-llvm/main.md: compile times typically 10--20x faster than the LLVM -O0 back-end with similar execution time; code size ~10-30% larger for -O0 IR and similar for -O1 IR.
corrections.caveats: Compile-time win only; generated code is -O0 quality, not comparable to V8 TurboFan, HotSpot C2 or LLVM -O2. TPDE-LLVM supports a subset of LLVM-IR (x86-64-v1 and AArch64 Armv8.1 ELF only; Clang -O2 and higher IR typically fails on unsupported vector operations and falls back to the full LLVM back-end); code size 10-30% larger for -O0 IR. The README cites only the arXiv preprint 2505.22610; the peer-reviewed version is CGO 2026 (Schwarz, Kamm, Engelke) with an artifact on Zenodo (record 17619677) running SPEC CPU 2017, which is proprietary, so the evaluation is not fully reproducible. Paper numbers are snippet only and differ by version: arXiv snippet says 8-24x faster than LLVM -O0 on SPEC CPU 2017 with geomean 12.15x (x86-64) and 18.96x (AArch64) and run time within +-9%; the CGO snippet says 8-26x, geomean 16.2x/18.7x over -O0 and 85.8x/80.0x over -O1. The search agent's Wasmtime/Cranelift figures (4.27x faster compile than Cranelift, Cranelift code 1.64x faster) were not re-checked.

notes: Record accurate; README and docs carry the 10-20x figure, paper only via snippets (blocked hosts), so B rests on the CGO 2026 acceptance and Zenodo artifact seen in search results. Shortcomings: -O0 code quality only, LLVM-IR subset with fallback, SPEC-based evaluation not reproducible, paper not opened. Candidate for a paper-access retier check (arXiv 2505.22610 or home.cit.tum.de/~engelke/pubs/2602-cgo1.pdf).

tier_reason: README numbers (Coremark 5x faster compile and 39% faster code, PolyBenchC 6.5x and 63% versus Chrome's Liftoff) match the peer-reviewed OOPSLA 2021 copy-and-patch paper (Distinguished Paper), whose abstract per search snippet reports 4.9x-6.5x faster compilation and 39%-63% faster code than Liftoff. Not A: the repo's harness (test_parser.cpp: WasmCompilation.BenchmarkAll, WasmExecution.CoremarkWasiBenchmark, PolyBenchC_*) times only WasmNow, the Liftoff side (Chrome version, flags) is not in the repo, and no CPU model is stated; the paper PDF was not opened.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: clang++ 10.0.0 (LLVM 10.0.0 release binaries installed in dockerfile/Dockerfile on Ubuntu 18.04); production flavor adds -O3 -DNDEBUG, plus -pthread -mavx2 (CMakeLists.txt); built via pochivm-build cmake/make production. Liftoff/Chrome version and flags not stated in the repo.
corrections.caveats: Peer-reviewed support is the OOPSLA 2021 paper 'Copy-and-Patch Compilation' (Xu and Kjolstad, Distinguished Paper Award); its abstract per search snippet gives 4.9x-6.5x faster compilation and 39%-63% faster generated code than Liftoff on Coremark and PolyBenchC, matching the README; the PDF was not opened (fredrikbk.com, sillycross.github.io, arXiv blocked; no copy in the sillycross.github.io repo). The repo benchmark harness (test_parser.cpp) measures WasmNow only; Liftoff measurements and the CPU model are not in the repo. Beats Liftoff, a baseline tier, not V8's optimizing TurboFan. Research prototype: 4 commits, last in Oct 2021; WebAssembly 1.0 core only with partial WASI (runs Coremark and PolyBenchC, other modules may hit unimplemented imports); requires AVX2 (-mavx2); the author warns not to run untrusted WebAssembly with it (unaudited JIT, sandbox-escape risk).

notes: Record accurate; claims match README and the paper abstract (snippet). Shortcomings: Liftoff side not reproducible from the repo, no CPU model, abandoned 2021 research prototype with partial WASI and an explicit security warning, beats only the baseline tier. Copy-and-patch technique later adopted by CPython's JIT (separate entry).

tier_reason: Upgraded C to A: the What's New numbers link to the 2026-09-25 doesjitgobrrr run, whose raw data is public in savannahostrowski/pyperf_bench (results/bm-20260925-3.16.0a0-80f9aa0-JIT/...-ripley-x86_64-...-vs-base.md: overall geometric mean 1.079x faster), run with pyperformance 1.14.0 via bench_runner (bench_runner.toml), and the pyperf JSON metadata states the compiler (GCC 13.3.0, -O3), configure flags (--enable-optimizations --with-lto=full --enable-experimental-jit=yes) and CPU (Intel Core i5-8400 @ 2.80GHz, turbo off, performance governor). The macOS AArch64 run states Clang 21.0.0 and flags but no CPU model.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Python 3.15 What's New (Doc/whatsnew/3.15.rst): 7-8% geometric mean pyperformance improvement for the JIT over the standard interpreter built with all optimizations on x86-64 Linux; 11-12% over the tail-calling interpreter on AArch64 macOS; per-benchmark JIT vs no-JIT from roughly 15% slowdown to over 100% speedup, ignoring unpack_sequence. Linked raw run (pyperf_bench, commit 80f9aa0, 2026-09-25): x86-64 overall geometric mean 1.079x faster (vs-base.md). From the run's pyperf JSONs (derived from page data, 105 benchmarks after bench_runner exclusions): x86-64 geomean 1.075x, per benchmark 0.89x (k_core) to 2.47x (richards_super); macOS arm64 JIT+tail-call vs tail-call geomean 1.113x, 0.82x (k_core) to 2.23x (richards); the excluded unpack_sequence runs 0.56x (x86-64) and 0.71x (macOS), i.e. slower with the JIT.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: x86-64 Linux run: GCC 13.3.0, CFLAGS -O3 -DNDEBUG -fno-omit-frame-pointer -mno-omit-leaf-frame-pointer, configure --enable-optimizations --with-lto=full (PGO+LTO) with and without --enable-experimental-jit=yes. macOS arm64 run: Clang 21.0.0 (clang-2100.1.1.101), same configure flags plus --with-tail-call-interp on both sides. JIT stencils are generated at build time with LLVM 21 (Tools/jit/README.md). Flags from pyperf JSON metadata in savannahostrowski/pyperf_bench.
corrections.hardware: x86-64: Intel Core i5-8400 @ 2.80GHz (6 cores, intel_pstate no turbo, performance governor), Linux 6.8.0, glibc 2.39 (runner 'ripley'). AArch64: Apple Silicon Mac on macOS 26.5.2 (runner 'jones'; CPU model not recorded in metadata).
corrections.workload: pyperformance 1.14.0 suite run by bench_runner (13 benchmarks excluded from the geomean, including unpack_sequence, pickle and asyncio_tcp), JIT-enabled build versus the same CPython commit (main, 3.16.0a0, 80f9aa0, 2026-09-25) built without the JIT.
corrections.caveats: Compares the JIT with CPython's own interpreter, not with PyPy, LuaJIT, V8 or HotSpot, so it does not beat the jits category baselines; the gain is small (7-12% geomean) and some benchmarks slow down (k_core 11-18% slower; unpack_sequence, excluded from the geomean, about 1.4-1.8x slower, derived from the run's JSON). The JIT is still experimental and off by default (--enable-experimental-jit). Numbers come from a main-branch 3.16.0a0 build (commit 80f9aa0, 2026-09-25), not a 3.15 release binary. Runs are by a CPython core developer's own runners (savannahostrowski/pyperf_bench, doesjitgobrrr.com dashboard, which was blocked here); the macOS runner's CPU model is not recorded. Included as a flagged entry for the copy-and-patch lineage (stencils built with LLVM 21). License file is the Python license stack (PSF License Version 2 and predecessors, SPDX Python-2.0) plus 0BSD for documentation code; GitHub shows it as Other.
